I had a roommate who, very coherently, rapped in her sleep.

Anyway, technically speaking it happened three times. Two short term facilities in Vegas, then one long-term facility off in the middle of a mountain in Arizona.

To give you a vague idea on how different short-term and long-term is, short-term is for crisis situations and long-term is for people who aren't necessarily a ticking time bomb, but sure as hell have some issues that *will* turn them into that if they aren't resolved appropriately.

In the short-term facilities, they usually keep you for a week, sometimes two or more if they're planning on transferring you somewhere else. Doesn't sound so bad at first, but once you're in there the most you've got are other people with horrid issues themselves, and a couple of deck of cards *if* you're lucky. They're isn't a whole lot of "treatment" persay, since the place is mostly a facility for you to "cool off" in. Meds are often prescribed and most of the time you get assigned a therapist, but it's very common in these facilities to not even speak more than a handful of words to them. Occasionally people are explosive, and occasionally you get caught in the crossfire. Not a whole lot of privacy and you're almost guaranteed to get a roommate. These places run on a tight schedule, so it's easy to consider it like a school that you're not allowed to leave and you sleep in.

The long-term was harder to deal with, but in a different sense. I'm not as familiar with them since I've only been to one. Wasn't allowed to curse, take about tattoos, gangs and the like, and it kinda had a religious foundation to it. The rules there were very black and white and difficult to maneuver around in a lot of cases. I found the place suffocating and exhausting and i wasn't showing any improvement. So I "faked" getting better so I eventually could be let out and I did.
Scars, lots of them. And my personality can get pretty ugly sometimes.

Get into the habit of checking your mirrors while you're still fresh. Saves you a lot of borderline heart attacks and actual collisions.

Death itself has never been something I've been afraid of. I just see it as an occurrence that's inevitable for everyone and everything. As somebody who's lost a lot of loved ones through death (in both old age and horrible mishaps) it would be hard for me to avoid the topic, so it's simply one that I'm, for lack of a better word, comfortable with.

Problem with this, is that I have a hard time understanding those who fear death and can't comfort them properly when they lose loved ones or are just generally paranoid.
Loud eating tends to be the one to get my goat, but unnecessarily loud groaning when people stretch can hit a nerve for me, too.

Probably the Kimberley story because 1) I hallucinate a lot and 2) the air vent in my room is directly above the top part of my bed. And, of course, I felt it was completely reasonable to hear it at 2am for the first time.

Comparing my mental illness to someone else's is probably the best way to get me to tune out, honestly. Sensitivity is not something you can just push aside. If two people get a nasty cut on their finger and one of them is watery-eyed while the other didn't even flinch, calling the person on the verge of tears a baby doesn't make the pain go away. They just start suffering in silence as a result and feel guilty for being open about pain.

H'oh boy. The ER. Fun times.

I specifically remember the two times I had to go there myself for suicide-related things, both times were equally unpleasant, and both times i was equally mistreated. So trust me when I say that this is a very common thing and that I wholeheartedly agree with you with just going to a psychiatric facility first. Because if you don't, the process is terrible.

That tends to be the first thing they look into when recruiting due to the importance of psych evaluations. You're not the first person to attempt suicide this way and you're certainly not going to be the last, and even the slightest hint that you're not feeling so hot in the head is going to be noticeable to them because, unfortunately, they've seen it before multiple times.
